panels.title: Orders accepted / s
panels.description: Orders that were persisted as PENDING and announced to Kafka. This is the load the rest of the pipeline has to absorb.

panels.title: Orders completed / s
panels.description: Orders reaching a terminal status, PAID or FAILED. Steadily below the accepted rate means the pipeline is falling behind.

panels.title: Paid share (5m)
panels.description: Of the orders that finished in the last five minutes, the share that was paid. The load generator aims a small share at an unreservable SKU, so a few percent of failures is the expected baseline.

panels.title: Pipeline p95
panels.description: 95th percentile of the time from an order being accepted to it reaching PAID or FAILED — the whole chain, two Kafka hops included.

panels.title: Orders in flight
panels.description: Orders that have been accepted but have not finished, counted in the database. A number that climbs and does not come back down is the first sign of a stalled consumer.

panels.title: Consumer lag (broker)
panels.description: Total unread records across every consumer group, as the broker sees it. Zero means consumers are keeping up.

panels.title: Pipeline throughput
panels.description: Each stage of the chain as a rate. In a healthy system the three lines sit on top of each other; a gap between created and completed is work piling up somewhere in between.

panels.title: Orders in flight by status
panels.description: Accepted orders that have not finished yet, counted in the database. PENDING is waiting on stock, RESERVED on payment — so the shape of this panel says which consumer is the bottleneck. Terminal orders are left out; they only ever accumulate.

panels.title: End-to-end latency
panels.description: Accepted → terminal, measured inside the service across all three consumers. The load generator polls a sample of orders and reports the same figure from the outside, as a cross-check.

panels.title: Stage latency (p95)
panels.description: Where the time goes: reserve is created → stock reserved, payment is reserved → charged. Payment carries the simulated provider latency, so it is normally the larger of the two.

panels.title: Failure reasons
panels.description: Why orders fail, bucketed. insufficient_stock is the reservation refusing; payment_declined covers both a rejected charge and a call the open circuit breaker never made.

panels.title: Stock remaining
panels.description: Units left per product in the in-memory ledger. It is never replenished, so a long run drains it — and every further order for that product fails on reservation.

panels.title: Dead-lettered records
panels.description: Records parked in .DLT topics after exhausting their retries. Anything above zero is a poison message worth looking at.

panels.title: POST /orders by response
panels.description: 202 is an accepted order. 409 is a business key that was already used — the idempotency guard doing its job, and expected traffic while the load generator is replaying keys on purpose.

panels.title: POST /orders latency
panels.description: Percentiles computed by Prometheus from histogram buckets, not averaged from per-instance summaries. Covers only the synchronous part: validate, insert, respond.

panels.title: Requests in flight
panels.description: Requests currently being served. Growing while latency grows means the connector is saturated rather than the work being slow.

panels.title: GET /orders/{id} by response
panels.description: Status polling. The load generator follows a sample of the orders it places, so this tracks --follow-share of the accepted rate.

panels.title: Database query time

targets.expr: sum by (repository, method) (rate(spring_data_repository_invocations_seconds_sum[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (repository, method) (rate(spring_data_repository_invocations_seconds_count[$__rate_interval]))

panels.description: Mean time per repository call. Every stage of the pipeline reads and writes an order, so this is the floor under all of it.

panels.title: Consumer lag by group (broker)
panels.description: Stop a consumer and this climbs; start it again and it drains. The metric a real on-call rotation alerts on.

panels.title: Consumer lag by client (application)
panels.description: The same pressure reported by the Kafka client inside the JVM. Present even without kafka-exporter, but blind while the app is down. The topic filter drops Kafka's deprecated period-replaced duplicates (orders_reserved alongside orders.reserved), which would otherwise double the sum.

panels.title: Listener throughput
panels.description: Records processed per second by each @KafkaListener. Each one runs spring.kafka.listener.concurrency threads, one per partition.

panels.title: Listener latency (p95)
panels.description: How long one record takes to handle, per listener. Multiply by the record rate and compare against the thread count to see how close a listener is to saturation.

panels.title: Topic write rate
panels.description: Records appended per second, per topic — the production side of the pipeline, as the broker sees it.

panels.title: Producer send / error / retry
panels.description: The application's own producer. Retries are usually harmless — idempotent sends make them safe — but a persistent rate means the broker is struggling to accept writes.

panels.title: Payment circuit breaker state
panels.description: One series per state, holding 1 while that state is active. Raise APP_PAYMENT_FAILURE_RATE to watch it flip to open.

panels.title: Payment calls by outcome
panels.description: successful / failed / not_permitted. Calls rejected outright by an open breaker show up as not_permitted — they cost nothing and never reach the provider.

panels.title: Circuit breaker window
panels.description: Resilience4j's own view of its sliding window. -1 means the window has not yet seen the minimum number of calls, so the breaker cannot trip yet. Buffered calls share the axis but are a count, not a percentage.

panels.title: Payment call duration
panels.description: Mean duration of a call through the breaker, by outcome. The simulated provider sleeps app.payment.latency-millis before answering, so successful calls sit just above that.

panels.title: JVM heap
panels.description: A sawtooth that keeps returning to the same floor is healthy. A floor that creeps upward under steady load is not.

panels.title: Garbage collection
panels.description: Seconds spent paused per second of wall clock. Anything approaching 0.1 means a tenth of the service's time is going to GC rather than to orders.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: Process CPU is this JVM's share of the machine. When it flattens near the core count while throughput stops rising, the service is CPU bound rather than waiting on Kafka or the database.

panels.title: Threads
panels.description: Blocked or waiting threads climbing under load points at contention — usually the connection pool or a lock, not the CPU.

panels.title: Database connections
panels.description: Pending is the one to watch: threads queued for a connection that the pool cannot hand out. Consumers and HTTP requests share this pool, so contention here slows down both.

panels.title: Log events
panels.description: Warnings and errors as a rate. A spike here usually explains a spike somewhere else on this page — payment fallbacks and dead-letter publications both log at warn or error.
